title: Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis

paper.title: Asynchronous LLM Post-Training: Group-Mass Capping and Convergence Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) improves the efficiency of large language model post-training but introduces stale rollouts generated by earlier policies. Theoretical understanding of how this staleness affects convergence and how to mitigate its impact remains limited. We derive a convergence bound for GRPO-style algorithms that explicitly characterizes the tradeoff between the gradient estimator’s second moment and bias. For trajectory-level importance-weighted estimators, our analysis shows that once the second moment is uniformly controlled, delay enters the bound through the bias introduced by clipping or rescaling. Guided by this insight, we propose a novel group mass capping GRPO (GMC-GRPO) method, which minimizes a ratio-based bias bound within a class of weighted estimators sharing a common second-moment guarantee. We establish convergence guarantees for asynchronous GMC-GRPO and show that, compared with TIC-GRPO, it improves the threshold dependence of the fourth-order delay term from O ⁡ ( ϵ − 4 ) O({\epsilon}^{-4}) to O ⁡ ( ϵ − 2 ) O({\epsilon}^{-2}) as ϵ → 0 {\epsilon}\to 0 , where 1 + ϵ 1+{\epsilon} is the ratio threshold. Under local policy overlap, the delay-dependent term decreases as G − 2 / 5 G^{-2/5} after tuning the step size, where G G is the group size. For fixed behavior and current policies, the bias introduced by group rescaling also vanishes as G → ∞ G\to\infty , whereas the bias from trajectory-wise clipping can persist. Experiments across Qwen3 models and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate improved robustness to stale rollouts, with GMC-GRPO achieving the best performance among stable baselines under large rollout delays.

sections.heading: 1 introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a widely used paradigm for post-training large language models (LLMs), enabling them to improve from outcome-level feedback rather than relying solely on static demonstrations ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Lambert et al., 2024 ) . Given a prompt, RL allows an LLM to generate thinking tokens before producing a final answer, and reinforces the generated trajectory based on its final quality ( Jaech et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Models post-trained with algorithms such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and its variants ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) have shown strong capabilities on challenging reasoning problems, such as math ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ; He et al., 2024 ) , coding ( Jain et al., 2025 ) , and agentic tasks ( Du et al., 2026 ) . To reduce the inefficiency of repeatedly alternating between rollout generation and policy optimization, modern RL training pipelines increasingly adopt asynchronous execution ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Such systems decouple rollout generation from policy optimization: rollout workers continuously generate responses using their local policy versions, while the learner updates the policy as soon as sufficient completed rollouts have accumulated and publishes the updated parameters without blocking generation ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Noukhovitch et al., 2025 ) . Together with optimized training engines and workload scheduling, this design allows inference and training to proceed concurrently, improving resource utilization and substantially increasing the training throughput of GRPO-style methods ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . The decoupling, however, introduces data staleness . Since rollout workers and the learner progress independently, the learner may update the policy several times before a generated rollout is consumed. Consequently, a training batch can mix trajectories collected under multiple earlier policy versions, creating a mismatch between the behavior policies that generated the data and the current policy being optimized ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . As the delay grows, these trajectories can become increasingly off-policy, making policy optimization more difficult and reducing training efficiency ( Tian et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Despite the empirical success of delay-aware algorithms ( Roux et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , how this staleness affects the convergence of GRPO-style algorithms, and how to mitigate its impact through principled algorithm design, remain poorly understood. This raises a natural but fundamental research question: Can we theoretically characterize how data staleness affects the convergence of GRPO-style algorithms, and use this to design RL algorithms better suited to asynchronous training systems? We answer this question by first identifying what any importance-weighted algorithm must control in order to converge, and then designing the correction that best meets this requirement under delay. Our key contributions are as follows: • Second moment and bias tradeoff. We derive a convergence bound for GRPO-style algorithms which explicitly captures the tradeoff between the second moment of gradient estimators and the bias error. With trajectory-level importance sampling, stale rollouts can produce large importance ratios and enlarge the gradient estimator’s second moment. Clipping these ratios controls the second moment but can introduce bias. When the resulting second-moment bound is independent of delay, delay enters the convergence bound through this clipping bias. This motivates algorithms that minimize a bias bound while maintaining a common second-moment guarantee. • GMC-GRPO. Guided by this principle, we introduce a class of weighted gradient estimators that satisfy a common second-moment bound. This class includes several GRPO-style methods as special cases. Within this class, we derive group mass capping (GMC)-GRPO by minimizing a bias bound and selecting a solution that preserves each group’s gradient direction, while retaining the same second-moment guarantee. This makes GMC-GRPO particularly well suited to asynchronous training, where its principled weighting rule effectively limits the bias. • Convergence of asynchronous GMC-GRPO. We establish a convergence guarantee for asynchronous GMC-GRPO with explicit dependence on stochastic rollout delays. Compared with TIC-GRPO ( Pang et al., 2025 ) , GMC-GRPO yields a strictly smaller delay-dependent penalty: in the tight-clipping regime, the penalty improves from O ⁡ ( ϵ − 4 ) O({\epsilon}^{-4}) to O ⁡ ( ϵ − 2 ) O({\epsilon}^{-2}) , where 1 + ϵ 1+{\epsilon} is the threshold for individual importance ratios in TIC-GRPO and their group average in GMC-GRPO. Moreover, because GMC-GRPO rescales a group only when its average importance ratio exceeds the stability cap, its correction bias vanishes as G G grows and the group average concentrates. In contrast, trajectory-wise clipping acts separately on every ratio, leaving a nonzero clipping bias even in the large-group limit. • Experiments. Finally, we evaluate GMC-GRPO under both controlled fixed delays and in a simulated asynchronous pipeline where rollout staleness is correlated with response length. Across Qwen3 models and reasoning benchmarks, GMC-GRPO achieves the best performance among vanilla GRPO-style algorithms and other baselines designed for asynchronous training. These results demonstrate effectiveness of our theory-guided design under asynchronous rollout delays. Related Work. We defer the comprehensive discussion of related work to Appendix A . Our paper is most closely related to off-policy correction for stale LLM rollouts in asynchronous RL systems ( Noukhovitch et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Typical strategies include adaptive clipping thresholds ( Roux et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , variance-aware step-size control ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , and reuse of stale experience through staged training with selective filtering or replay buffers ( Tian et al., 2026 ; Arnal et al., 2026 ; Ritter et al., 2026 ) . Despite the empirical success of these methods, few works have studied GRPO-style algorithms from a theoretical perspective, especially under asynchronous rollout delays. Zhou et al. (2026) characterize the GRPO gradient as a U-statistic and analyze its finite-sample error and dependence on group size, while Pang et al. (2025) introduce TIC-GRPO and provide the first rigorous convergence analysis of GRPO-style methods. Nevertheless, these studies are not under asynchronous training. More recently, Xu et al. (2026) analyze asynchronous GRPO through a generic biased-gradient framework, but leave the staleness-induced bias and higher-order remainder terms as abstract quantities in the final bound. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide an explicit delay-dependent convergence analysis of GRPO-style algorithms in asynchronous RL systems.

sections.text: As illustrated in Section 2.2 , we consider an asynchronous RL system in which multiple rollout workers generate responses continuously while a single learner updates the policy ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Noukhovitch et al., 2025 ) . Once all responses have been scored, the worker deposits the group and its behavior-policy version into a shared buffer. Delay plays a different role in Theorem 1 than in classical asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD) ( Tan et al., 2023 ; Maranjyan et al., 2025 ; Koloskova et al., 2022 ; Mishchenko et al., 2022 ) . In ASGD, an update applied at iteration n n is conditionally unbiased for the gradient at the stale iterate θ n − τ n \theta_{n-\tau_{n}} rather than at the current iterate θ n \theta_{n} , so staleness enters the descent argument directly through the discrepancy between the two gradients. In our setting, the trajectory-level ratio instead changes measure from the behavior policy π θ n − τ n ( b ) \pi_{\theta_{n-\tau_{n}^{(b)}}} to the current policy π θ n \pi_{\theta_{n}} , so the uncorrected estimator remains unbiased for ∇ J ​ ( θ n ) \nabla J(\theta_{n}) regardless of delay. Staleness instead enlarges the spread of the importance ratios, which makes a second-moment correction necessary; delay then affects the bound only through the bias of that correction as explained above. This difference also changes the appropriate remedy. ASGD commonly bounds staleness by discarding updates whose delay exceeds a threshold ( Tan et al., 2023 ; Maranjyan et al., 2025 ) , but the analogous gating in LLM post-training preferentially discards long responses and thus induces a length bias ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Improving the delay dependence therefore calls for RL algorithms that minimize the bias under the same second-moment control, which is precisely what group-mass-capping is designed to do.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate GMC-GRPO against several baselines: (i) vanilla GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ; (ii) GAC, which controls stale-aligned update directions through gradient projection ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ; (iii) VCPO, which combines effective-sample-size-guided step-size scaling with an off-policy minimum-variance baseline ( Huang et al., 2026 ) ; and (iv) TIC-GRPO ( Pang et al., 2025 ) . Among these methods, GAC and VCPO are designed specifically for asynchronous training. We first evaluate robustness under controlled fixed delays and then construct a simulated asynchronous system in which rollout delay is correlated with response length. Detailed parameter settings and implementation details are deferred to Appendix B.1 . We also discuss related approaches that selectively clip a fraction of importance ratios ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) and report an additional comparison with A-3PO ( Li et al., 2025 ) in Appendix B.2 . Controlled Fixed Delays. To isolate the effect of staleness, we evaluate GRPO, TIC-GRPO, and GMC-GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B under fixed rollout delays. Figure 2 reports sampled Pass@1 on MATH500 for delays of D = 0 , 64 , 128 D=0,64,128 learner updates; see Appendix B.1 . The full sweep over D ∈ { 0 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 , 512 } D\in\{0,32,64,128,256,512\} is deferred to Appendix B.2 . Without delay, all three methods attain similar final performance. At delay 64, GMC-GRPO learns faster than TIC-GRPO and reaches comparable final Pass@1, with both outperforming vanilla GRPO. At delay 128, GMC-GRPO achieves 59.03% Pass@1, compared with 55.41% for TIC-GRPO and 35.33% for vanilla GRPO. These results show that GMC supports faster learning and stronger final performance as staleness increases. Simulated Asynchronous Delays. The fixed-delay study isolates staleness, but real rollout workers finish at different times: longer responses typically take longer to generate and thus reach the learner under older policies. To capture this coupling, we simulate an asynchronous pipeline in which rollout delay depends on generation length, producing heterogeneous delays averaging approximately 160 learner updates for Qwen3-1.7B and 140 for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. This setting tests whether GMC-GRPO remains robust when staleness varies across rollouts. Among the methods reported in Table 1 , GMC-GRPO achieves the highest mean avg@ n n scores across all three model sizes (41.47, 56.20, and 59.62) and the highest mean greedy scores on Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B (48.77 and 64.37). On Qwen3-4B, its mean greedy score of 60.63 is 0.83 points below TIC-GRPO. Notably, GMC-GRPO also outperforms the two of the most recent asynchronous-RL stabilization methods: GAC, which controls stale-aligned update directions via gradient projection, and VCPO, which combines ESS-guided step-size scaling with a minimum-variance baseline. Both improve over vanilla GRPO under delay but remain below TIC-GRPO-style trajectory correction at 4B and 8B. These results indicate that the robustness of group-mass capping is not restricted to fixed delays, but holds under heterogeneous, length-dependent staleness. sections.heading: 6 Conclusions and Limitations
sections.text: This work studies how rollout staleness affects the convergence of GRPO-style algorithms in asynchronous LLM training and introduces GMC-GRPO to improve learning from delayed rollouts. Our theory and experiments show that group-level capping improves robustness to stale rollouts while maintaining performance on fresh data. Within the proposed class of weighted gradient estimators, our analysis provides a foundation for understanding and improving delay tolerance. Future work can extend this framework to more general weighting rules, such as those that use information beyond importance ratios, to further improve the balance between second-moment control and bias.

sections.heading: Appendix A Related Work
sections.text: Asynchronous RL Systems for LLM Post-Training. LLM RL pipelines typically alternate between autoregressive rollout generation and policy optimization, incurring idle time from variable response lengths and repeated switches between inference and training ( Zhong et al., 2024 ; Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Recent work improves this pipeline along two main directions. Asynchronous RLHF and LLM RL systems decouple rollout generation from policy optimization so that the two stages can proceed concurrently ( Noukhovitch et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . Complementary approaches improve rollout-side utilization through continuous grouped sampling or scale exploration and learning through asynchronous replay ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Bartoldson et al., 2026 ) . This decoupling, however, causes the learner to consume trajectories generated by lagged behavior policies, making rollout staleness an intrinsic off-policy optimization issue. Rather than proposing another systems architecture, we aim at finding robust algorithms against data staleness in asynchronous RL systems: we analyze GRPO-style optimization under stochastic rollout delays and design an importance correction that controls the resulting bias without sacrificing stability. Off-Policy Correction for Stale LLM Rollouts. Stale rollouts can induce heavy-tailed importance ratios, allowing a small number of trajectories to dominate the gradient estimate and destabilize training. Learning from such data therefore requires a careful choice of how the update is corrected. Existing corrections differ mainly in where they intervene. A common strategy acts locally on individual ratios: TIC-GRPO clips a trajectory once its ratio exceeds the clipping threshold ( Pang et al., 2025 ) , while related methods replace fixed clipping with tapered weights, adaptive or asymmetric thresholds, and entropy-scaled trust regions ( Roux et al., 2025 ; Xi et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . A second strategy controls batch- or update-level statistics through second-moment constraints, variance-aware step sizes, or gradient-alignment control ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . A third changes how stale experience is reused through staged training with selective filtering, replay buffers, or objectives designed for lagged inference policies ( Tian et al., 2026 ; Arnal et al., 2026 ; Ritter et al., 2026 ) . Together, these methods show that stale data can remain informative when its effect on the update is controlled. Our work instead moves from individual correction to group-level control. We identify a cap on corrected importance mass that preserves gradient second-moment bound and derive a uniform rescaling rule that reduces delay-induced bias without selectively clipping trajectories. Theory of GRPO-Style Optimization under Delay. The convergence theory of asynchronous optimization is well developed, with rigorous and tight convergence analysis that matches the lower bound under various settings ( Joulani et al., 2013 ; Koloskova et al., 2022 ; Mishchenko et al., 2022 ; Tyurin et al., 2026 ) . In parallel, a growing line of work establishes theoretical guarantees for RL-based LLM post-training ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025b ; Foster et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025a ) . Despite this progress, most existing RL-for-LLM theories are developed within the natural policy gradient and RLHF frameworks, and rigorous convergence guarantees for widely used GRPO-style algorithms remain limited, particularly under asynchronous rollout generation. Zhou et al. (2026) characterize the GRPO gradient as a U-statistic and analyze its finite-sample error and dependence on group size, while Pang et al. (2025) introduce TIC-GRPO and provide the first rigorous convergence analysis of GRPO-style methods. More recently, Xu et al. (2026) analyze asynchronous GRPO through a generic biased-gradient framework, but leave the staleness-induced bias and higher-order remainder terms as abstract quantities in the final bound. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide an explicit delay-dependent convergence analysis of GRPO-style algorithms in asynchronous RL systems.

sections.heading: B.1 Detailed Experiment Setup
sections.text: Models and training data. We run the experiments with the Qwen3-1.7B-Base, Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base models ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . All methods update the full actor; we use neither LoRA adapters nor an explicit KL-divergence penalty. The training set is constructed from the seven subject-specific training splits of MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) : algebra, counting and probability, geometry, intermediate algebra, number theory, prealgebra, and precalculus. After removing examples for which the reference answer cannot be extracted, the resulting training set contains 7,498 problems. Training and evaluation use the same two-shot prompt, which instructs the model to reason step by step and place its final answer in \boxed{} . Shared training configuration. We generate rollouts with vLLM ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) in BF16, using temperature 1.0 1.0 and top- p = 1.0 p=1.0 . Prompts and completions are truncated at 1,024 and 4,096 tokens, respectively. Each rollout mini-batch contains eight prompts and eight responses per prompt, for a total of 64 trajectories. Except for the zero-delay runs in the fixed-delay suite described below, we set inner_steps=1 , so these 64 trajectories produce one actor update. We optimize with 8-bit AdamW ( Dettmers et al., 2021 ) , a learning rate of 10 − 6 10^{-6} , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , and zero weight decay. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule with a 3% warmup, and the gradient norm is clipped at 1.0 1.0 . We use a mix of NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation GPUs and NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPUs for training, depending on resource availability. Controlled fixed delays. The fixed-delay study uses Qwen3-1.7B-Base and sweeps the delay over D ∈ { 0 , 32 , 64 , 128 , 256 , 512 } D\in\{0,32,64,128,256,512\} optimizer updates. For D = 0 D=0 , we use inner_steps=4 , so each rollout batch comprises four 64-trajectory optimizer mini-batches, for 256 responses in total. For every D > 0 D>0 , we use inner_steps=1 and maintain a FIFO queue of D D 64-trajectory rollout batches. The queue is initialized with batches generated by the initial policy. In these delayed runs, at each learner iteration, the oldest batch is consumed in one optimizer update and a new batch from the current policy is appended, yielding a steady-state behavior-policy lag of D D optimizer updates after the initial fill transition. All remaining optimization, rollout, and sequence-length settings match the shared configuration above. Figure 3: A full version of Figure 2 with delay=0, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512. The second suite models the coupling between response length and asynchronous rollout latency. We maintain a hidden in-flight buffer and a virtual clock τ \tau . Launching a 64-trajectory rollout batch advances the clock by C gen = 85 C_{\mathrm{gen}}=85 . If the batch has mean completion length L L , it becomes visible at τ ready = τ launch + λ ​ L , λ = 28 . \tau_{\mathrm{ready}}=\tau_{\mathrm{launch}}+\lambda L,\qquad\lambda=28. Each optimizer update advances the clock by C update = 1 C_{\mathrm{update}}=1 , and ready batches are exposed in completion-time order. Thus, longer batches tend to be consumed under older learner policies. A batch generated at optimizer step g g and consumed at step t t has realized delay d = t − g d=t-g ; its approximate steady-state mean is 𝔼 ⁡ [ d ] ≃ λ ​ 𝔼 ​ [ L ] C gen + C update = 28 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ L ] 86 . \mathbb{E}[d]\simeq\frac{\lambda\,\mathbb{E}[L]}{C_{\mathrm{gen}}+C_{\mathrm{update}}}=\frac{28\,\mathbb{E}[L]}{86}. Consequently, λ \lambda controls the delay distribution, while the measured mean delay—approximately 160 updates in the reported experiments—also depends on the model’s response-length dynamics. At initialization, we launch rollouts from policy 0 until the first batch is visible. If the visible queue later becomes empty, we launch the minimum number of additional batches needed to expose the next sample; both warmup and refill use a safety cap of 400 launches. For Qwen3-1.7B, rollout generation and actor updates execute sequentially on one GPU. For Qwen3-4B, one GPU serves vLLM rollouts and a second GPU performs actor optimization, with rollout generation overlapped with learner updates. This systems-level overlap does not alter the sample order or the simulated-delay schedule. Remark 6 ( Scope of the asynchronous-sampling assumption ) . The fixed-delay suite satisfies Assumption 3 exactly, since every group’s delay is fixed in advance and independent of its responses. The simulated suite intentionally relaxes the conditional-independence part of the assumption: because delay is determined by response length, conditioning on a long delay tilts the returned responses toward longer completions. Our theorems therefore do not formally cover this setting. The key mechanism behind Assumption 3 is nevertheless preserved. The pipeline is lossless, so response length changes only when a rollout is consumed, not whether it is consumed, and each importance ratio uses the exact behavior policy that generated the rollout. As a result, the length–delay coupling largely averages out over the course of training, unlike completion-time filtering, which systematically removes long responses. Moreover, this coupling makes the problem harder rather than easier: long responses are both more stale and more prone to extreme importance ratios. We therefore view the simulated suite as a stress test beyond the idealized assumption, and GMC-GRPO’s robustness there suggests that its advantage does not hinge on this idealization. Method-specific settings. Vanilla GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) uses the two-sided clipping range ϵ = 0.2 \epsilon=0.2 and the unnormalized group-centered advantage r i − r ¯ g r_{i}-\overline{r}_{g} . VCPO ( Huang et al., 2026 ) uses effective-sample-size-guided step-size scaling and its closed-form off-policy minimum-variance baseline. GAC ( Xu et al., 2026 ) uses cosine-similarity thresholds 0.05 0.05 and 0.30 0.30 . TIC-GRPO ( Pang et al., 2025 ) and GMC-GRPO both use leave-one-out advantages, ϵ high = 0.28 \epsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28 . All other training, rollout, data-order, and delay parameters are held fixed across methods within each suite. Evaluation. For the simulated asynchronous study, we evaluate the step-800 checkpoint on six mathematical-reasoning benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 problems) ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) , GSM8K (1,319) ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , Gaokao2023-Math-En (385) ( Liao et al., 2024 ) , the OE_TO_maths_en_COMP subset of OlympiadBench (674) ( He et al., 2024 ) , Minerva Math (272) ( Lewkowycz et al., 2022 ) , and AMC23 (40) ( Art of Problem Solving, 2024 ) . Both suites use the same 1,024-token prompt limit, 4,096-token generation limit, two-shot prompt, and last-complete- \boxed{} answer scorer as in training.

We therefore report this comparison separately and discuss the observed instability in detail. To make use of stale rollouts without overly restricting policy updates, A-3PO follows decoupled policy optimization ( Fu et al., 2026 ) : it uses a proximal anchor for clipping while retaining importance correction relative to the behavior policy. Suppressing token arguments ( y t ∣ x , y < t ) (y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t}) , the decoupled surrogate is L decoupled CLIP ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ π prox π θ behav ​ min ⁡ { π θ π prox ​ A ^ , clip ⁡ ( π θ π prox , 1 − ϵ , 1 + ϵ ) ​ A ^ } ] , L_{\mathrm{decoupled}}^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\pi_{\mathrm{prox}}}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{behav}}}}\min\!\left\{\frac{\pi_{\theta}}{\pi_{\mathrm{prox}}}\widehat{A},\,\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}}{\pi_{\mathrm{prox}}},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)\widehat{A}\right\}\right], (10) where the expectation is over sampled rollout tokens and A ^ \widehat{A} is the group-based advantage. Under large delays, however, α \alpha approaches zero, so the ratio used for clipping can remain close to one and the update can resemble unclipped GRPO . Since the outer importance factor π prox / π θ behav \pi_{\mathrm{prox}}/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{behav}}} remains unclipped, large importance weights can destabilize updates and even lead to training collapse in extreme cases. This is also demonstrated in our experiments: Table 5 shows that A-3PO outperforms GMC-GRPO on Qwen3-1.7B in mean greedy/mean avg@ n n accuracy (49.16/45.27 versus 48.77/41.47). Retaining more of these signals can therefore improve performance when extreme importance ratios are rare. The Qwen3-8B experiment illustrates the accompanying stability challenge. In Figure 6 , A-3PO initially learns faster but its training reward collapses around step 430, whereas GMC-GRPO continues to improve and reaches mean greedy/mean avg@ n n accuracy of 64.37/59.62. This trajectory resembles the prosperity-before-collapse behavior reported by Zheng et al. (2026) , where removing the trust region exposes useful stale-data signals but also permits destabilizing updates. The comparison highlights the motivation for GMC: preserving learning signals must be coupled with control of update magnitude. GMC caps the average importance mass within each group and preserves the relative contributions of its responses, controlling the update second moment under the assumptions of Proposition 1 .
